Port-Transversal Barriers: Graph-Theoretic Safety
for Port-Hamiltonian Systems
Chi Ho Leung and Philip E. Par ´e*
Abstract—We study port-Hamiltonian systems with energy
functions that split into local storage terms. From the inter-
connection and dissipation structure, we construct a graph on
the energy compartments. From this graph, we show that the
shortest-path distance from a constrained compartment to the
nearest actuated one gives a lower bound on the relative degree of
the corresponding safety constraint. We also show that no smooth
static feedback can reduce it when no path exists. When the
relative degree exceeds one and the immediate graph neighbors
of the constrained compartment is connected to at least one
input port, we reshape the constraint by subtracting their shifted
local storages, producing a candidate barrier function of relative
degree one. We then identify sufficient regularity conditions that
recover CBF feasibility under bounded inputs. We validate the
framework on an LC ladder network, where the enforceability of
a capacitor charge constraint depends only on the input topology.
Index Terms—Port-Hamiltonian Systems, Control Barrier
Functions, Energy-based Safety
I. INTRODUCTION
Safety constraints in port-Hamiltonian systems—joint limits
in robotics, charge bounds in electrical networks, pressure caps
in fluid systems—often depend only on non-actuated state
components, resulting in relative degree greater than one with
respect to the input. The standard CBF-QP safety filter [1],
[2] is inapplicable in this setting, since the input does not
appear in the first-order time derivative of the barrier. For
mechanical systems, the energy-aware barrier which subtracts
kinetic energy to restore relative degree one [3]. However,
the construction is tied to canonical mechanical coordinates.
It does not address which structural features make it work,
whether it generalizes beyond mechanics, or when the result-
ing CBF inequality is feasible under bounded inputs.
Port-Hamiltonian systems (PHS) provide a natural setting
for answering the aforementioned questions. In standard port-
Hamiltonian (PH) ODEs, topology fixes the interconnection,
dissipation, and input structure, while the Hamiltonian defines
the efforts that drive flows through that structure. In this work,
we focus on systems with separable storage across energy
compartments, which is the standard setting in bond-graph and
Dirac-structure modeling [4, Ch. 2].
The PHS structure suggests that barrier feasibility should
admit a topological characterization independent of any partic-

the central question of this work as:
How can we leverage the known topology of a
port-Hamiltonian system to generalize energy-aware
barrier design for non-mechanical settings, without
requiring higher-order derivatives?
We answer this question in two steps. We first show that
the relative degree of a safety specification is lower-bounded
by the shortest-path distance, in the influence graph, from
constraint-bearing to input-carrying compartments. This pro-
vides a purely topological diagnostic for arbitrary graph dis-
tance and identifies a structural obstruction when no path
exists. We then turn our attention to the energy-shaping
problem of a barrier function: when the constraint nodes admit
a local input-carrying blanket, we reshape the specification by
subtracting shifted local storages from that blanket, yielding
aport-transversal barrierof relative degree one. The present
synthesis addresses the case where the blanket neighbors al-
ready carry input ports. Under three additional feasibility-side
conditions, along with the standing structural and compactness
assumptions, we further show that the resulting CBF inequality
is enforceable under bounded inputs.
Related Works and Contributions
Control Lyapunov and control barrier functions are now
widely combined in QP-based safety-critical control to jointly
encode stabilization and forward invariance [5]. In parallel,
passivity-based methods [6] provide a natural control-design
framework for physical systems admitting a PH representation.
More recently, energy-aware CBFs [3] have emerged as a
promising alternative for safety-critical control in mechani-
cal systems, showing that energy-based barrier constructions
can bypass repeated higher-order differentiation [7], [8] by
exploiting physical structure instead. However, existing results
are largely tied either to mechanical coordinates or to energetic
interpretations of already chosen barriers [9]–[11]. This leaves
open the question of whether energy-aware barrier shaping can
be derived from structure alone for a broader class of PHS. The
present work takes a first step in that direction by providing:
(i) a graph-theoretic diagnosis of relative-degree obstruction,
(ii) a constructive reshaping rule based on a barrier-insulating
blanket, and (iii) feasibility guarantees under bounded inputs.

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document introduces a graph-theoretic approach to ensuring safety in port-Hamiltonian systems (PHS) by developing "port-transversal barriers." The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Standard Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) are often inapplicable to PHS when safety constraints depend on non-actuated states, leading to a relative degree greater than one with respect to the input. Existing energy-aware methods are often limited to mechanical systems.
*   **Approach:** The paper leverages the topological structure of PHS, specifically the interconnection and dissipation structure, to construct an "influence graph" on energy compartments.
*   **Key Findings:**
    *   The shortest-path distance in the influence graph from a constrained compartment to the nearest actuated one provides a lower bound on the relative degree of the safety constraint.
    *   If no path exists between a constrained compartment and an actuated one, smooth static feedback cannot reduce the relative degree.
    *   When the relative degree exceeds one and the immediate neighbors of a constrained compartment are connected to input ports, the constraint can be reshaped by subtracting shifted local storages. This creates a "port-transversal barrier" with a relative degree of one.
*   **Contributions:**
    *   A graph-theoretic diagnosis for relative-degree obstruction in PHS.
    *   A constructive method for reshaping safety specifications into relative-degree-one barriers based on a "barrier-insulating blanket."
    *   Feasibility guarantees for the resulting CBF inequality under bounded inputs, given certain regularity conditions.
*   **Methodology:** The analysis relies on the system's structure (interconnection, dissipation, and input matrices) and assumes separable storage Hamiltonians and structural regularity.
*   **Validation:** The framework is validated on an LC ladder network, demonstrating that the enforceability of a capacitor charge constraint depends solely on the input topology.

5.  **Numerical Validation:** An example using an LC ladder network demonstrates the effectiveness of the framework. It shows that a "port-insulated" barrier (where all blanket nodes are also port nodes) leads to enforceable safety, while a non-port-insulated barrier results in constraint violations.

In essence, the document provides a graph-theoretic approach to analyze safety constraints in PHS, determine their inherent difficulty (relative degree), and systematically construct a modified safety specification (port-transversal barrier) that can be effectively enforced by control inputs, with clear conditions for success.
